name: The 'noble' man versus 'slave morality'
plain_explanation: Nietzsche distinguishes an aristocratic ethic, fit only for a superior few, that prizes pride, strength, and the capacity for cruelty ('noble' morality) from the morality actually preached by Christianity and democratic movements, which Nietzsche calls 'slave morality' -- a moral code he says was invented by the weak and resentful to tame and control the strong.
precise_definition: Nietzsche's aristocratic ethical framework: true virtue belongs only to a governing minority (the 'noble' man), who recognizes duties only to equals, may act with cruelty toward inferiors, and embodies the incarnate will to power; this is opposed to Christian/democratic 'slave morality,' which Nietzsche diagnoses as the ideological product of resentment among the 'bungled and botched,' aiming to break the spirit of the strong by converting 'their proud assurance into anxiety and conscience-trouble.'
why_it_mattered: It is the ethical center of the chapter and the doctrine Russell subjects to the most sustained criticism, since it explicitly denies that 'the happiness of common people is no part of the good per se.'
historical_origin: Beyond Good and Evil and Thus Spake Zarathustra.
examples: Nietzsche calling ordinary human beings 'the bungled and botched'
'No morality is possible without good birth'
The 'noble' man will protect artists and craftsmen while recognizing duties only to equals
objections: Russell: this requires defining the 'superior few' either as congenitally superior (a biological claim Russell treats skeptically) or as products of education/environment (in which case excluding others from the same advantages is hard to justify).
Russell: it never occurred to Nietzsche that his 'noble' man's lust for power is itself rooted in fear, whereas those who have genuinely conquered fear feel no need to tyrannize.
competing_positions: Bentham's principle of the greatest happiness of the greatest number, which Russell notes is compatible with an aristocratic form of government but not with Nietzsche's aristocratic ethic, since Bentham (unlike Nietzsche) holds the happiness of the many is intrinsically good
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes 'many modern developments' connected to this outlook are, in fairness to Nietzsche, 'contrary to his clearly expressed opinions' -- an explicit caution against over-hasty identification of Nietzsche's views with later political movements.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly and extensively targets Christianity as the ideological vehicle of 'slave morality.'
